en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on the Defeats (Pārājikakaṇḍa)
2. The Second Pārājika Training Rule At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Now at that time, a number of monks who were friends and companions, having built grass huts on the slope of Mount Isigili, entered upon the rains retreat there.
The venerable Dhaniya, the potter’s son, also built a grass hut and entered the rains retreat.
Then, when those monks had completed the rains retreat at the end of the three months, they dismantled their grass huts, put away the grass and wood, and set out on a journey through the countryside.
But the venerable Dhaniya, the potter’s son, remained right there for the rains, and there for the winter, and there for the summer.
Then, while the Venerable Dhaniya the potter’s son had entered the village for alms, grass-gatherers and wood-gatherers broke down his grass hut and went away taking the grass and wood.
A second time, the Venerable Dhaniya the potter’s son gathered grass and wood and built a grass hut.
A second time, as the venerable Dhaniya the potter’s son had entered the village for alms, grass-cutters and wood-gatherers broke down his grass hut and departed taking the grass and wood with them.
A third time, the venerable Dhaniya the potter’s son gathered grass and wood and built a grass hut again.
A third time, as the Venerable Dhaniya the potter’s son had entered the village for alms, grass-gatherers and wood-gatherers broke down his grass hut and went away taking the grass and wood.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Dhaniya the potter’s son:
“As many as three times, while I have been entering the village for alms, grass-gatherers and wood-gatherers have broken down my grass hut and gone away taking the grass and wood.”
“I am indeed well-trained and experienced in my own ancestral craft of pottery, having mastered the art thoroughly.
What if I were to knead clay myself and build a small hut entirely made of clay?
Then the Venerable Dhaniya, the potter’s son, kneaded clay himself, built a small hut entirely made of clay, gathered grass, wood, and cow dung, and fired that hut.
That hut was beautiful, lovely to behold, pleasing, and red, just like an *indagopaka* insect.
Its sound was just like the sound of a *kiṅkaṇika* bell.
Then the Blessed One, descending from Vulture Peak Mountain together with many bhikkhus, saw that hut—beautiful, lovely to behold, pleasing, and red.
Having seen it, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, what is this that is so beautiful, lovely, pleasing, and red, like an *indagopaka* insect?
Then those bhikkhus reported the matter to the Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“It is unbecoming, monks, for that foolish man; it is unsuitable, improper, unworthy of a recluse, unallowable, and not to be done.
How indeed, monks, can that foolish man build a hut made entirely of clay?”
"Indeed, monks, there can be no compassion, pity, or harmlessness toward living beings for that foolish man.
Go, monks, break up this hut.
Let not future generations fall into the practice of drinking blood."
“Monks, a hut made entirely of clay must not be built.
Whoever should build one commits an offense of wrong-doing.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One, and they went to where that hut was; having arrived, they demolished that hut.
Then the Venerable Dhaniya Kumbhakāraputta said this to those bhikkhus:
“Friends, why are you tearing down my hut?
“Friend, the Blessed One is having it torn down.”
“Break it, friend, if the Master of the Dhamma himself orders its destruction.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Dhaniya, the potter’s son:
“Up to three times now, when I have entered the village for alms, grass-gatherers and wood-gatherers have broken my grass hut and gone away taking the grass and wood. What shall I do?”
“Even this little hut made entirely of clay that I built has been demolished by the Blessed One.
Now, I have a trusted accountant at the timber-yard.
What if I were to ask the accountant for timber and build a wooden hut?”
Then the Venerable Dhaniya Kumbhakāraputta went to the foreman at the timber yard; having approached him, he said this to the foreman:
"Friend, three times now I have entered the village for alms and grass-carriers and wood-carriers have come, having broken down my grass hut and taken away the grass and wood.
Even that little hut made entirely of clay by me has been caused to be demolished by the Blessed One."
“Give me some wood, friend;
I wish to build a wooden hut.
“Venerable sir, there is no such wood as that which I might give to you, my lord.”
“Venerable sir, there are logs for the repair of the city, set aside for use in times of emergency.
If the king has them given, venerable sir, please have them brought.
“They have been given by the king, friend,” he replied.
Then it occurred to the householder accountant at Dārugaṇaka:
"These ascetics, followers of the Sakyan son, are practitioners of the Dhamma, practitioners of integrity, practitioners of the holy life, speakers of truth, virtuous, and of beautiful character.
The king, too, has full confidence in them."
"One ought not to say that what was given was not given.
Then the accountant at the timber yard said to the Venerable Dhaniya Kumbhakāraputta,
"Please take it, Bhante."
Then the Venerable Dhaniya Kumbhakāraputta had those logs cut into small pieces, had them hauled out by carts, and built a wooden hut.

Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, while inspecting the works in Rājagaha, went to the foreman of the timber-yard; having approached him, he said this to the foreman of the timber-yard:
"Those [logs], my good man..."
“Where are those timber logs for the city’s repairs, which were set aside by the King for use in times of emergency?
“Sir, those timber logs were given by the King to the venerable Dhaniya, the potter’s son.
Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, was displeased.
“How can it be that the King will give to Dhaniya the potter’s son the timber from the royal forest, which was set aside for the repair of the city and intended for times of emergency?
Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, approached King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha; having approached, he said this to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha:
“Is it true, Sire, that the timber for the city repairs, which was set aside by Your Majesty for times of need, has been given to Dhaniya the potter’s son?
“Who says so?
“The treasurer at the timber store, Sire.”
“In that case, brahmin, order the accountant at the timber storehouse.
Then Vassakāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, ordered the bound accountant at the timber storehouse to be brought forth.
The Venerable Dhaniya Kumbhakāraputta saw the accountant being led away from the timber storehouse in bonds.
Having seen him, he said this to the accountant at the timber yard:
"Friend, why are you being led away as a prisoner?
"It is on account of those logs, venerable sir."
“Go, friend; I too shall come.
“Please come, venerable sir, before I am killed.
Then the Venerable Dhaniya Kumbhakāraputta went to the residence of King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha approached the Venerable Dhaniya, the potter’s son; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Dhaniya, the potter’s son, and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha said this to the Venerable Dhaniya, the potter’s son:
“Is it true, venerable sir, that I gave to you noble sir those ‘divine-grasp’ logs, which had been set aside for the repair of the city and for times of emergency?”
“Yes, Great King.
“Venerable sir, we who are called kings have many duties and much to do;
even after giving, we might not remember it.”
“Please, venerable sir, remind me.
“Do you remember, Great King, that when you were first consecrated, you spoke these words:
‘Let the ascetics and brahmins enjoy only the grass, wood, and water that have been given to them’?”
“I do, Bhante.
There are, Bhante, some recluses and brahmins who are modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training;
even on account of a minor matter, scruple arises in them.”
"It was with reference to them that I spoke, and specifically to those in the forest who are unencumbered.
On that basis, venerable sir, you imagine you may take wood that has not been given.
For how could one such as I kill, bind, or banish a recluse or a brahmin living within his own domain?"
“Go, venerable sir; you have been released by your hair.
Do not do such a thing again.
Thus did the people criticize, grumble, and spread it about.
“Shameless are these recluses, sons of the Sakyan; they are immoral and speakers of falsehood.
For how can they claim to be practitioners of the Dhamma, practitioners of integrity, practitioners of the holy life, speakers of truth, virtuous, and of beautiful character?
They possess neither the state of a recluse nor the state of a brahmin.”
The state of a recluse is lost for these; the state of a brahmin is lost for these.
From where can they have the state of a recluse? From where can they have the state of a brahmin?
These have departed from the state of a recluse; these have departed from the state of a brahmin.
“They deceive even kings; how much more so other men!
The monks heard those people complaining, grumbling, and lamenting.
Those monks who were of few desires, contented, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training, complained, grumbled, and lamented:
“How indeed could the venerable Dhaniya Kumbhakāraputta take wood belonging to the king that was not given?
Then those monks, having rebuked the venerable Dhaniya Kumbhakāraputta in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having assembled the community of monks, questioned the venerable Dhaniya Kumbhakāraputta:
“Is it true, Dhaniya, that you took wood belonging to the king without it being given?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him.
“Mendicant, this is unbecoming, improper, unsuitable, unworthy of a recluse, unallowable, and not to be done.
How, mendicant, could you take wood belonging to a king that has not been given?
This, mendicant, does not lead to the inspiration of those without faith, nor to the increase of those with faith.”
“Now, foolish man, this will lead to a lack of confidence in those who have no confidence, and to the alienation of some of those who already have confidence.
At that time, a certain former high official who had gone forth among the monks was sitting not far from the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One said this to that monk:
“By how much, monk, does King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha punish a thief when he has him seized—by execution, imprisonment, or banishment?
“By a quarter, Blessed One, or by a quarter of a quarter.
Now at that time, a *pāda* in Rājagaha was worth five māsakas.
Then the Blessed One, having rebuked the Venerable Dhaniya, the potter’s son, in many ways for being difficult to support … [as before] … And furthermore,
monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever monk should take what has not been given, considering it as theft, [is one who has committed an offense].”

“In whatever manner of taking what is not given kings, having seized a thief, would execute him, imprison him, or banish him, saying: ‘You are a thief, you are a fool, you are deluded, you are a robber’—if a bhikkhu takes what is not given in such a manner, he too is defeated and no longer in communion.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks went to a dyer’s workshop, stole a dyer’s bundle of goods, brought them to the monastery,
and divided them among themselves. The other monks said, “Friends, you are truly very meritorious!”
“Much robe-cloth has been acquired for you.
“From where, friend, could we have merit?
Just now we went to a laundry and stole a washerman’s bundle.”
“Friend, has not a training rule been laid down by the Blessed One?
For what reason, friend, did you steal a dyer’s bundle?
“It is true, friend, that a training rule was laid down by the Blessed One.”
“And that, moreover, was in the village, not in the forest. “Surely, friend, it is just so.
This is unbecoming, friend; it is unsuitable, improper, unworthy of a recluse, unallowable, and not to be done.”
"How is it, friends, that you would steal a dyer’s bundle?
This, friends, is neither for the inspiration of those without confidence nor for the increase of those with confidence;
rather, friends, it leads to the lack of confidence in those without confidence and to the alienation of some among those with confidence."
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having convened the Saṅgha of monks, questioned the group-of-six monks:
“Is it true, monks, that you went to a dyer’s workshop and stole a dyer’s bundle?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“It is unseemly, foolish men, it is unbecoming, improper, unworthy of a recluse, unallowable, and not to be done.”
"How indeed, you foolish men, could you steal a dyer's bundle?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence, nor to the increase of the confidence of those who already have it;
rather, foolish men, it leads to the lack of confidence of those without confidence, and to the alienation of some among those who have confidence."
Then the Blessed One, having rebuked the group of six monks in many ways for their difficult-to-support nature … [as before] … having spoken in praise of the arousal of energy,
and having given a Dhamma talk to the monks that was appropriate and conducive thereto, addressed the monks:
“… And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus— ”

“Furthermore, whatever monk should take from a village or from a forest what has not been given, constituting theft, such that kings, having seized a thief for an act of taking what is not given, would execute him, imprison him, or banish him, saying:

‘You are a thief! You are a fool! You are deluded! You are a robber!’—a monk who takes what has not been given in such a manner is also one who has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.”
"But whoever" means whoever such as this...
"a monk."
...pe... this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu.
A village is called a village whether it consists of a single hut, two huts, three huts, four huts, or even if it has inhabitants.

A village: a village inhabited by non-humans, a village that is enclosed, a village that is unenclosed, a village where cattle and goats reside, and even a caravan that has stayed for more than four months—this too is called a village.
What is called the vicinity of a village?
The range of a stone’s throw by a medium-sized man standing at the city gate of an enclosed village;
or the range of a stone’s throw by a medium-sized man standing in the vicinity of the houses of an unenclosed village.
This is called "forest."
Excluding both the village and the vicinity of the village, the remainder is called the forest.
"What is not given" means that which is not given, not relinquished, not abandoned, guarded, protected, cherished as "mine," and possessed by another. This is what is called "not given."
"Intended as theft" means with a mind of theft, a mind intent on taking away.
"Should take" means—
One might take it, carry it away, steal it, disturb its posture, move it from its place, or pass beyond the agreed signal—
whether it be a certain amount of money, or what is worth a foot, or more than a foot.

"Kings" refers to universal monarchs, regional kings, provincial rulers, those who hold intermediate territories, those who oversee districts, high ministers, or whoever else governs by inflicting punishments such as cutting or breaking. These are called "kings. A "thief," on the other hand, is...
Whoever takes what has not been given, which is reckoned as theft, having a value of five māsakas or more than five māsakas— that person is called a thief.
"They might kill him" means they might kill him with a hand, or a foot, or a whip, or a cane, or a switch, or by cutting him.

"Or they might bind him" means they might bind him with a rope-bond, or a chain-bond, or a shackle-bond, or a house-bond, or a city-bond, or a village-bond, or a town-bond, or they might place him under guard.
"Or they might banish him" means...
Whether from villages, market towns, cities, districts, or parts of districts, they might banish one, saying:
"You are a thief! You are a fool! You are deluded!
You are a robber!"—this is mere abuse.
"Such a thing as a quarter-measure, or what is worth a quarter-measure, or more than a quarter-measure.
"Taking it" means...
"Taking," "carrying away," "removing," "disturbing the deportment," "displacing from its place," and "passing the signal"—
these too are said [in relation to the previous] by way of reference to what precedes.
“He becomes one who has committed a pārājika offense” means:

just as a withered leaf, once detached from its stalk, is incapable of becoming green again, even so a bhikkhu, having taken what is not given—whether it be a foot, the value of a foot, or more than a foot—in the manner of theft, ceases to be a samaṇa and ceases to be a son of the Sakyans. Therefore, it is said: “he becomes one who has committed a pārājika offense.”
"Non-residence":
"residence" means performing the formal acts together, reciting the scriptures together, and training under the same rules. This is what is called "residence.
He does not have that [residence] with him; therefore it is called "non-residence."

Land situated on the ground, land situated on dry ground, land situated in the air, land situated in the sky, land situated in water, land situated in a boat, land situated in a vehicle, land situated as a burden, land situated in a park, land situated in a monastery, land situated in a field, land situated on a building site, land situated in a village, land situated in a forest; water; a tooth-stick; a tree; a portable article;
a deposit; a toll-gate; a living being; a footless creature; a two-footed creature; a four-footed creature; a many-footed creature.
Carrying about, guarding, exchanging, making a signal, and making a sign.
"Goods stored on the ground" means goods that have been placed on the ground, dug into, or concealed.

If, with a thieving mind, thinking "I will steal property standing on the ground," he seeks out a companion, or seeks out a spade or a basket, or goes [to the spot], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he cuts wood or a creeper growing there, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he digs up soil there, or heaps it up, or lifts it out, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he touches the jar, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he makes it move, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If he causes it to fall from its place, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
If, with a thieving mind, he inserts his own vessel [into another's] and touches it when it is worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he makes it move, there is an offense of grave transgression (thullaccaya).
If he makes it enter his own vessel or breaks off a handful [of the contents], there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
If, with intent to steal, he touches an article strung on a thread—whether it be an earring, a neck-thread, a waist-thread, a cloth, or a turban—he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he makes it move, he commits a serious offense (thullaccaya).
If, having grasped it by the end, he lifts it up, he commits a serious offense (thullaccaya).
If he shakes it and takes it out, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
If he releases even as much as a hair’s breadth from the mouth of the jar, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
If, with a mind intent on theft, he drinks ghee, oil, honey, or molasses—worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas—in a single act, there is an offense entailing defeat.
If he breaks it right there, or discards it, or burns it, or renders it unusable, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
"Goods situated on dry land" means goods that have been placed on dry land.
If, with a thieving mind, thinking "I will steal land-based goods," he searches for a companion or goes [to the site], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he touches them, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he makes them move, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If she causes it to fall from its place, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
"Property situated in the air" means property that has gone into the air.

Whether it be a partridge, a francolin, a partridge, or a quail; or whether it be a cloak, a turban, silver, or gold—when these fall while being cut, if one with a thieving mind thinks, "I shall steal this object situated in the air," and either searches for a companion or goes [to do so], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he interrupts his progress, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she makes it quiver, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If she causes it to move from its place, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
"Goods left on high" means they have gone to a height. They are hung upon a bed,
or a chair, or a clothes-peg, or a clothes-line, or a wooden post, or a wall-nail, or a tree, or even upon a bowl-rest.
Thinking, "I will steal property left out in the open," if one with a thieving mind seeks out a companion or goes toward it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one touches it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one makes it move, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If she causes it to be moved from its place, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
"Water-dependent goods" means goods that have been placed in water.
If, with a thieving mind, thinking "I will steal goods situated in water," one seeks out a companion or goes [to the spot], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Whether one dives in or surfaces, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches [the goods], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he makes it tremble, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If he moves it from its place, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).

In this regard, if with a mind of theft he touches a water-born lotus—whether a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white lotus—or a lotus-root, or a fish, or a tortoise, if it is worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she makes it shake, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If she moves it from its place, there is an offense of pārājika.
"A boat" means:
That by which one crosses.
"Goods placed on a boat" means goods that have been put onto a boat.
Thinking, “I will steal goods that have not been left behind,” if one with a thieving mind seeks out a companion or goes [to the place], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one touches it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one makes it move, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If he causes it to move from its place, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
If, with a thieving mind, thinking "I will steal the boat," he either searches for a companion or goes toward it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he touches it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she makes him writhe, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If she releases his bonds, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
Having released his bonds, if she touches him, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
If he causes it to move, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If he moves it upward, downward, or across, even by as much as the breadth of a hair, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
What is called "a vehicle"?
A cart, a chariot, a wagon, or a carriage.
"Goods for transport" means goods that have been placed upon a vehicle.
If, with a thieving mind, thinking "I will steal goods belonging to a caravan," he either searches for a companion or goes [toward them], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he touches [the goods], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he makes them move, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If he displaces it from its place, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
If, with a thieving mind, thinking "I will steal the vehicle," he searches for a companion or goes toward it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he touches it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she makes it quiver, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If she causes it to move from its place, there is an offense of pārājika.
"A load" means:
A load on the head, a load on the shoulder, a load on the waist, or a hanging load:
if one touches a load on the head with a thieving mind, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one makes it move, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If he causes the load to fall off, it is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
If, with a mind of theft, he touches the load on its shoulder, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he makes it move, it is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If he lowers his waist-cloth, it is an offense of defeat (pārājika).
If, with a mind of theft, he touches a load on the waist, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he makes it move, it is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If he takes it with his hand, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
If, with intent to steal, he places the burden from the hand onto the ground, there is an offense entailing expulsion.
If, with intent to steal, he takes it from the ground, there is an offense entailing expulsion.
"Arāma" means a flower garden or a fruit garden.
"The meaning of arāma" means:
Property in a monastery is placed in four locations: on the ground, on dry land, in the air, or suspended in space.
If, with a thieving mind, thinking "I will steal the property located in the monastery," one seeks out a companion or goes toward it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one touches it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he shakes it, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If he moves it from its place, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
In that regard, if with a mind of theft he touches a root, bark, leaf, flower, or fruit growing there, worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she makes it tremble, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If she causes it to move from its place, there is an offense of pārājika.
If she attacks the monastery, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
If she causes doubt to arise in her husband’s mind, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If the husband, thinking “I will no longer be her husband,” abandons his responsibility, there is an offense of pārājika.
If, while practicing the Dhamma, she defeats her husband, there is an offense of pārājika.
If one who is practicing the Dhamma steals it, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
"Property kept in a monastery" means property placed in a monastery in four ways: kept on the ground, kept on dry land, kept in the air, or kept in the open space.
If, with a thieving mind, thinking "I will steal the goods belonging to the monastery," he seeks out a companion or goes [toward them], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he touches them, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he makes them shake, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If she causes [the owner] to move from his place, it is an offense of defeat (pārājika).
If she makes a formal claim against the monastery, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she creates doubt in the mind of the owner, it is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
Thinking, "My husband will no longer be mine," she gives up her burden; there is an offense of defeat (pārājika).
If, while acting according to the Dhamma, she defeats her husband, there is an offense of defeat.
If, while acting according to the Dhamma, she is defeated, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).

Monks, perceiving it to be discarded rags (*paṃsukūla*), had it offered to them and consumed it.
Those bandits then accused those monks:
“You are no longer ascetics!
They became anxious... [as before] ...
“There is no offense, monks, for one who perceives it as a rag-robe.”
Now at that time, in the Andhavana grove near Sāvatthī, some bandits, having killed a pig, eaten the meat, and put away what remained, departed.
The monks, perceiving it to be discarded refuse (paṃsukūla), had it formally offered to them and consumed it.
Those bandits then reproached those monks:
“You are no longer ascetics.
They became anxious... [as before] ...
“There is no offense, monks, for one who perceives it as a rag-robe.”
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu went to a field of grass and, with a thieving mind, took away cut grass worth five māsakas.
He became anxious... [as before] ...
"Bhikkhu, you have fallen into an offense entailing defeat."
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu went to a grass field, cut some grass, and, with a thieving mind, took it, worth five māsakas.
He felt remorse... [as before] ...
"Bhikkhu, you have fallen into an offense entailing expulsion."
Now at that time, visiting monks, having had mangoes distributed by the Saṅgha, consumed them.
The resident monks censured those monks,
saying, "You are not ascetics!"
They became anxious...
[as before] ...and they reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"What were you thinking about, monks? he asked.
“For the purpose of consumption, Blessed One.
“There is no offense, monks, for the purpose of consumption.
Now at that time, visiting monks [offered] a rose-apple tree to the Saṅgha…
A labuja fruit for the Saṅgha… a jackfruit for the Saṅgha… a ripe palmyra fruit for the Saṅgha…
Having had sugarcane for the Saṅgha...
and timbarūsaka fruit for the Saṅgha distributed, they consumed them.
The resident monks censured those monks.
“You are not ascetics,” he said. They became anxious... [and so on] ...
“There is no offense, monks, for the purpose of consumption.”
Now at that time, the Ambapālaka people were giving mango fruits to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus, being scrupulous, did not accept them, thinking, "These people are masters; they are not ones to give."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“There is no offense, monks, in giving to a cowherd.
Now at that time, there were mango-guards...
...custodians of *labuja* fruits...
custodians of *panasa* fruits...
custodians of ripe *tāla* fruits...
The sugarcane guardians...
the *timbarūsaka* guardians gave *timbarūsaka* fruit to the monks.
The monks thought, “These people are masters for the purpose of guarding; they are not here to give.”
Feeling guilty, they did not accept it.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"There is no offense, monks, in giving to a cowherd," [the Blessed One said].
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, having taken wood for the Sangha on loan, used it to support the wall of his own dwelling.
The bhikkhus rebuked that bhikkhu, saying,
"You are no longer a samaṇa!"
He became anxious and reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"With what state of mind were you, monk? he asked.
“I am using it for a limited time, Blessed One.
“There is no offense, monk, when it is used for a limited time.
Now at that time, a certain monk, with a mind of theft, took water belonging to the Saṅgha.
With a thieving mind, he took clay belonging to the Saṅgha...
with a thieving mind, he took grass that had been piled up for the Saṅgha...
he became anxious... [and so on]...
“You have fallen, monk, into an offense entailing defeat.
Now at that time, a certain monk, with a mind of theft, burned a heap of grass belonging to the Saṅgha.
He became anxious... [as before]...
“There is no offense, monk, for a pārājika;
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Now at that time, a certain monk, with a thieving mind, stole a bed belonging to the Saṅgha...
He became anxious... [as before] ...
"Monk, you have committed an offense entailing expulsion.
Now at that time, a certain monk [stole] a bench belonging to the Saṅgha...
A mattress for the Saṅgha … a pillow for the Saṅgha … a door-panel for the Saṅgha …
He took away the Sangha’s window-opening ...
he took away the Sangha’s rafter with a thieving mind ...
he felt remorse ... [etc. ...
“You have fallen, monk, into an offense entailing defeat.
Now at that time, monks were using a dwelling belonging to a certain lay follower as their own lodging.
Then that lay follower complained, grumbled, and became indignant:
“How indeed, Venerable Sir, could they consume it as one thing and consume it as another?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, what is consumed as one thing must not be consumed as another.”
"Whoever should use it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, being afraid of wrongdoing, the monks sat on the bare ground when they were taking the Uposatha hall or the assembly hall;
their limbs and their robes became covered in dust.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to take it for a limited time,” he said.
Now at that time, in Campā, a nun who was a pupil of the nun Thullanandā went to a family that supported the nun Thullanandā.
“Noble lady, you wish to drink rice gruel with three kinds of molasses,” she said;
having had it cooked and brought, she consumed it herself.
When the other found out, she reproached her.
“You are no longer a female ascetic.
She became anxious... [as before] ...
Then that bhikkhunī reported this matter to the bhikkhunīs.
The bhikkhunīs reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“There is no offense, bhikkhus, involving a pārājika.”
“There is an offense of expiation for a deliberate lie.
Now at that time, a nun who was a pupil of the nun Thullanandā went to a family supported by the nun Thullanandā and said,
“The Noble Lady wishes to eat honey-balls.”
Having had it cooked and brought back, she consumed it herself.
When the other woman found out, she reproached her,
saying, "You are no longer an ascetic!"
She became anxious... [as before] ...
"There is no offense, monks, for a pārājika;
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for intentional lying."
Now at that time, in Vesālī, the householder who was the supporter of the Venerable Ajjuka had two children—a son and a nephew.
Then that householder said to the Venerable Ajjuka:
"Venerable sir, please point out this place to whoever among these two children has faith and confidence."
Now at that time, the householder’s nephew was faithful and confident. Then the Venerable Ajjuka pointed out that opportunity to the boy.
With that inheritance, he established a household and began giving alms.
Then the householder’s son said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Venerable Ānanda, who indeed is the heir to a father—the son or the nephew?
“The son, friend, is the heir to the father.
“Venerable sir, this noble Ajjuka has told our property to our paramour.”
“Friend, the venerable Ajjuka is no longer a monastic.
Then the venerable Ajjuka said this to the venerable Ānanda:
“Friend Ānanda, give me a judgment.”
Now at that time, the Venerable Upāli was on the side of the Venerable Ajjuka.
Then the Venerable Upāli said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Friend Ānanda, if someone is told by his master, 'Point out this place to such-and-such a person,' and he points it out to him, what offense does he commit?"
“Venerable sir, he does not commit anything, not even a mere *dukkaṭa* offense.
“Friend, this venerable Ajjuka was told by his employer, ‘Point out this place to such-and-such a person,’ and he pointed it out for him.
There is no offense, friend, for the venerable Ajjuka.”
Now at that time, in Bārāṇasī, the family that supported the Venerable Pilindavaccha was being harassed by thieves;
two children had been carried off.
Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha brought those children back by means of his psychic power and placed them upon the palace roof.
When the people saw those children,
they thought, "This is the power of the psychic majesty of the venerable Pilindavaccha," and they gained deep confidence in the venerable Pilindavaccha.
The bhikkhus criticized, grumbled, and complained,
saying, “How can the venerable Pilindavaccha bring back children who have been carried off by thieves?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“There is no offense, monks, for one who possesses psychic power within the domain of psychic power.
Now at that time there were two monks who were friends, Paṇḍuka and Kapila;
one was staying in a village, and the other was staying in Kosambī.
Then, as that bhikkhu was traveling from the village to Kosambī, while crossing a river on the way, a piece of fat released from the hands of some pork-butchers became stuck to his foot.
The bhikkhu took it, thinking, “I will give this back to its owners. The owners then accused him.
“You are no longer a recluse!
When he had crossed over, a cowherd girl saw him and said this:
“Come, venerable sir, let us engage in sexual intercourse.”
Thus, thinking, “By nature I am no longer a recluse,” he engaged in sexual intercourse with her.
Having gone to Kosambī, he reported this matter to the monks.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“There is no offense, monks, for the taking of what is not given that constitutes a *pārājika*;
there is an offense of *pārājika* for engaging in sexual intercourse.

Now at that time, a monk who was a student of the Venerable Daḷhika in Sāgalā, being oppressed by lack of faith in the spiritual life, stole a turban from a shopkeeper and said this to the Venerable Daḷhika:
“I am no longer a monastic, venerable sir; I shall disrobe.
“What have you done, friend?
He explained the matter to him.
Having had it brought, he had it appraised.
While it was being appraised, it did not even amount to five māsakas.
“There is no offense, friend, of a pārājika,” [he said].
He gave a discourse on the Dhamma.
"That bhikkhu delights [in it].
The second Pārājika is finished.
